{{short description|Surface in three-dimensional space}} 
[[Image:Ruled hyperboloid.jpg|thumb|right|300px|A string model of a portion of a regulus and its opposite to show the rules on a hyperboloid of one sheet]]
In three-dimensional space, a '''regulus''' ''R'' is a set of [[skew lines]], every point of which is on a [[transversal (combinatorics)|transversal]] which intersects an element of ''R'' only once, and such that every point on a transversal lies on a line of ''R''.

The set of transversals of ''R'' forms an '''opposite regulus''' ''S''. In <math>\mathbb{R}^{3}</math> the union ''R'' ∪ ''S'' is the [[ruled surface]] of a [[hyperboloid of one sheet]].

Any 3 skew lines generate a pair of reguli:<ref>[[H. S. M. Coxeter]] (1969) ''Introduction to Geometry'', page 259, [[John Wiley & Sons]]</ref>

# The set of lines that intersect all 3 of them sweeps out a quadratic surface. This ruling of this quadratic surface is the regulus.
# The set of lines that intersect all lines in the regulus is the ''complementary regulus'' or ''associated regulus'', by [[Skew lines#Gallucci's theorem|Gallucci's theorem]].

Any 3 lines in a regulus generate the complementary regulus, and vice versa. The regulus surface is the unique quadratic surface that contains these 3 lines. The pair of reguli sweep out the same surface, showing that it is a [[doubly ruled surface]].

According to [[Charlotte Scott]], "The regulus supplies extremely simple proofs of the properties of a conic...the theorems of Chasles, [[Brianchon's theorem|Brianchon]], and [[Pascal's theorem|Pascal]] ..."<ref>Charlotte Angas Scott (1905) [https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1905-12-01/S0002-9904-1905-01279-9/S0002-9904-1905-01279-9.pdf The elementary treatment of the conics by means of the regulus], [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 12(1): 1–7</ref>

In a [[finite geometry]] PG(3, ''q''), a regulus has ''q'' + 1 lines.<ref>[[Albrecht Beutelspacher]] & Ute Rosenbaum (1998) ''Projective Geometry'', page 72, [[Cambridge University Press]]  {{ISBN|0-521-48277-1}}</ref> For example, in 1954 [[William Edge (mathematician)|William Edge]] described a pair of reguli of four lines each in PG(3,3).<ref>[[W. L. Edge]] (1954) "Geometry of three dimensions over GF(3)", [[Proceedings of the Royal Society]] A 222: 262–86 {{doi|10.1098/rspa.1954.0068}}</ref>

[[Robert J. T. Bell]] described how the regulus is generated by a moving straight line. First, the hyperboloid <math>\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} \ = \ 1</math> is factored as
:<math>\left(\frac{x}{a} + \frac{z}{c}\right) \left(\frac{x}{a} - \frac{z}{c}\right) \ =\  \left(1 + \frac{y}{b}\right) \left(1 - \frac{y}{b}\right) .</math> 
Then the following two systems of lines, parametrized by &lambda; and &mu; satisfy that equation:
:<math>\frac{x}{a} + \frac{z}{c} \ =\ \lambda \left(1 + \frac{y}{b}\right), \quad \frac{x}{a} - \frac{z}{c} \ =\ \frac{1}{\lambda} \left(1 - \frac{y}{b}\right) </math> and 
:<math>\frac{x}{a} - \frac{z}{c} \ =\ \mu \left(1 + \frac{y}{b}\right), \quad \frac{x}{a} + \frac{z}{c} \ =\ \frac{1}{\mu} \left(1 - \frac{y}{b}\right) .</math>
No member of the first set of lines is a member of the second. As &lambda; or &mu; varies, the hyperboloid is generated. The two sets represent a regulus and its opposite. Using [[analytic geometry]], Bell proves that no two generators in a set intersect, and that any two generators in opposite reguli do intersect and form the plane tangent to the hyperboloid at that point. (page 155).<ref>[[Robert J. T. Bell]] (1910) [https://archive.org/details/elementarytreati033329mbp/page/n119 An Elementary Treatise on Co-ordinate Geometry of Three Dimensions], page 148, via [[Internet Archive]]</ref>
